claims.text: The proposed nanoparticles contain five transition metals at approximately 20 at.% each.
The initial HENA nanoparticles have grain sizes below 10 nm and can be synthesized by rapid quenching or sputtering.
CoCrFeMnNi or related five-metal nanoparticles can initially exhibit a single-phase FCC or BCC structure at room temperature.
Nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA nanoparticles may become structurally unstable at elevated temperatures.
Nanoparticle surface-energy effects may weaken configurational-entropy stabilization.
Elevated-temperature instability may cause accelerated atomic diffusion in HENA nanoparticles.
Surface-energy-driven diffusion and chemical short-range-order evolution may facilitate phase separation and grain coarsening.
High surface energy in nanoparticles may reduce the effective activation barrier for atomic diffusion.
Bulk high-entropy alloys exhibit a sluggish or hysteresis diffusion effect.
Nanoscale surface effects may counteract the sluggish-diffusion effect associated with bulk high-entropy alloys.
Accelerated diffusion may segregate elements into lower-energy phases, including BCC/FCC decomposition products.
Grain growth is driven by reducing total free energy through surface-area minimization.
Annealed nanoparticles may lose single-phase stability and form intermetallic or elementally segregated secondary phases.
Particles annealed at 700 K for 10 hours may undergo more than a 50% increase in grain size.
Bulk HENAs maintain single-phase structures and fine grains up to 1000 K.
The thermal stability of bulk HENAs arises from high configurational entropy, lattice distortion, and sluggish diffusion.
Nanoparticles larger than 50 nm should be dominated by bulk-like behavior.
Strong negative mixing enthalpies favor ordered phases and define a boundary where the proposed instability model may not apply.
Extreme pressure or irradiation can alter diffusion kinetics and invalidate the proposed model.
Experimental data on the finite-temperature behavior of HENA nanoparticles are limited, and available models may not capture particle-size and element-specific effects.
